title: Denoising under a data-processing ceiling: observer-dependent benefits, fidelity–task divergence, and an information floor
description:
A simulation study of when image denoising helps and when it hurts a detection task, under a fixed data-processing ceiling.

On synthetic signal-known-exactly phantoms spanning dose, noise correlation length and lesion configuration, three deterministic denoisers are evaluated against the analytic ideal-observer detectability of their own input (the ceiling) with a leakage-controlled, cross-fitted prewhitening observer, over ten independent realisations. The study quantifies three things: how often gains in reference-based fidelity (SSIM) coincide with losses in task detectability; how the effect of denoising depends on observer efficiency, comparing a prewhitening observer, a channelised Hotelling observer and a non-prewhitening observer; and how failure patterns — contrast erasure, excess lesion-like responses, task degradation — are distributed relative to an operational information floor, the acquisition contour at which the input's ideal-observer detectability falls below a prespecified task requirement (Rose, d' = 5). That floor is a task requirement, not a zero-information boundary.

Everything is synthetic, analytic and seeded; no patient data, no scanner calibration, and no absolute exposure thresholds are included. Model observers and the detection-task machinery are reused from taskiq-core.
